tagline: A wide stance pull with the hips close to the bar.

coaching.summary: Take a wide stance with toes turned out, grip the bar inside your knees, then push the floor apart and stand up tall.
cues: Stand wide with the toes out and the shins close to the bar.
Push the knees out over the toes and pull the slack out before the bar moves.
Drive the floor apart and keep the bar close all the way to lockout.

introduction.title: How the Sumo Deadlift Differs
paragraphs: The sumo deadlift is a deadlift with a wide stance and your hands inside your knees. Your feet turn out, your hips sit close to the bar, and your torso stays more upright than in a conventional pull.

That position shares the work differently. The quads and hips do more, the lower back does a little less, and the bar travels a shorter distance. Some lifters are built for it and pull their best lifts this way. Others are stronger conventional. Both are honest deadlifts.

Stand wide enough that your **shins are close to vertical** when you grip the bar, turn your toes out, and push your knees out over them. Pull the slack out of the bar, then think of pushing the floor apart as you stand up.
Log your sumo pulls and this page charts your rep PRs and tonnage, ready to read beside your [deadlift](/progress-guide/deadlift), so you can see which stance is moving.

faqItems.question: Is sumo or conventional deadlift stronger?
faqItems.answer: It depends on your build. Hip structure, leg length and torso length all play a part, and most lifters find one stance clearly more comfortable. Give each a fair run of a couple of months and let your logged numbers decide.

faqItems.question: How wide should my sumo stance be?
faqItems.answer: Wide enough that your shins are close to vertical when you look from the front, with your knees tracking over your toes. Start moderate and widen a little at a time. Your hips will tell you when you have gone far enough.

faqItems.question: Is the sumo deadlift easier on the lower back?
faqItems.answer: The more upright torso asks less of the lower back and more of the hips and quads. Many lifters rotate between stances for exactly that reason. It still rewards a flat back and a hard brace.

faqItems.question: Is the sumo deadlift allowed in powerlifting?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Sumo is a legal deadlift in powerlifting competition and plenty of records have been pulled that way. The bar still goes from the floor to a full lockout.

faqItems.question: Why is the sumo deadlift slow off the floor?
faqItems.answer: That is normal. Sumo is usually hardest at the start and quick once the bar passes the knees. Take the slack out, stay patient, and keep pushing the floor apart until the bar breaks.

faqItems.question: How often should I train the sumo deadlift?
faqItems.answer: Once or twice a week works for most lifters. You can make it your main pull, or train it beside your conventional [deadlift](/progress-guide/deadlift) as a second pulling day.
